newsitem.title: KENYA: IMF sees progress in Kenyan economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees progress in Kenyan economic reforms.

text.p: Kenya is likely to win delayed aid under an International Monetary Fund (IMF) soft-loans facility after progress in its privatisation programme and reform of the state pension agency, diplomats said on Thursday.
An IMF mission is in Kenya to review progress in reform and Kenyan officials are upbeat that a conclusion will be reached.
The IMF executive board will use the review for a final decision on whether to release the long-delayed second tranche when meeting in June or July, according to treasury officials.
IMF approved a three-year $220 million loan in 1996 under the soft-loans Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).

The first tranche of $37 million was released after the ESAF approval by the IMF executive board, but the second disbursement due last November was postponed, mainly due to what was seen as slow progress in critical reform areas such as privatisation.

"There is a reasonable chance of completion of discussions on the mid-term review and the second tranche disbursement thereafter if satisfactory measures are taken in the areas noted above," said IMF Resident Representative Reimer Carstens.
He said Kenya had macroeconomic issues under control.
"There has been progress. The cabinet has adopted several major bills related to the privatisation of the telecommunications sector and the power sector," he said.
Carstens said the new bills paved the way for a splitting of Kenyan Post and Telecommunications Corp (KPTC) into independent firms for post and telecommunications.
A supervising body and a contact office to be used by the government for liasing with the new companies would also be set up under the President's office, according to draft bills.

"They've done exactly what we've discussed for some time. What is important is that the telecommunications sector really is going to be fully privatised because telecommunications is key to the efficiency of the economy," Carstens told Reuters.
"The idea is to downsize the number of employees, pay them better salaries and make it more efficient," Carstens said.
Carstens said a bill on the power sector would lead to industry restructuring to allow for foreign partners with capital and knowhow to join in a partial privatisation.
The bills are awaiting debate and approval by parliament.
Carstens said Kenya had also made improvements in public enterprise reform and in public finances dicipline.

Western diplomats said another of Kenya's reforms to win praise was a bill reducing government involvement in the management of the state pension agency National Social Security Fund (NSSF), which has been accused of buying properties from politically-connected individuals at inflated prices.
